sentences.text: The skull was small, measuring only 60 mm in length and 30 mm in height, with very large elliptical orbits nearly as long as the rostrum, suggesting the animal might have been nocturnal.
The skull featured very large elliptical orbits nearly as long as the rostrum, suggesting the animal might have been nocturnal.
Its teeth were noticeably heterodont, featuring a mixture of incisiform, caniniform, and molariform types that supported its placement in the sphagesaurid group.
Despite its massive eyes, the entire body was only about 0.50 centimeters long.
The genus is known from a single holotype fossil collected by William Nava, which gives the species its specific name navae.
Remains were discovered in the Adamantina Formation near Marília, São Paulo, Brazil, during dam construction 25 km southwest of Marilia.
Excavations yielded approximately 7 specimens, mostly cranial material, some postcranial parts, and dozens of isolated bone elements.
Researchers suggest Adamantinasuchus might have had an omnivorous diet including plants, similar to Chimaerasuchus, due to its heterodont teeth and well-developed molariform teeth.

However, due to insufficient preservation of key jaw bones, it is debated whether Adamantinasuchus could chew plants; however, the lack of wear on its teeth suggests it was likely only capable of dorsoventral biting motions and ate softer food than plants.
Sharp front teeth were presumably used for cutting, while posterior molar-like teeth served for crushing.
Adamantinasuchus belongs to the suborder Notosuchia and is classified within the unranked family Ziphosuchia.
While occasionally classified in the family Sphagesauridae, some phylogenetic analyses suggest it is closely related to the genera Yacarerani or Pakasuchus rather than Sphagesaurus.

Adamantinasuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous period in Brazil, with fossils dating to the Turonian or Santonian ages, though the time range is recorded as Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago).
